theme: Doctrinal Pause: The Work of Christ, Atonement
summary: Christ’s death as substitutionary, propitiatory, and redemptive; the heart of the gospel
readingInstruction: Read Isaiah 53:1-12, then Romans 3:21-26, and then Hebrews 9:11-28. Today is a doctrinal pause, so you are reading three passages together: the prophet’s picture of the suffering Servant, Paul’s explanation of how God justifies sinners, and the author of Hebrews on the blood of Christ. Ask as you read: what exactly did Jesus accomplish on the cross, and how?
settingTheScene: You read Isaiah 53 yesterday. Today you read it again, alongside two New Testament passages that interpret it. Paul explains that God’s righteousness is shown in the cross and that sinners are justified by grace through faith. The author of Hebrews shows that Christ’s sacrifice fulfills and surpasses the Old Testament sacrifices. Together they give us the doctrine of the atonement, the work of Christ in dealing with sin.
observation: “He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5).
“The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6).
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 3:23-24).
“Whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith” (Romans 3:25).
“This was to show God’s righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins” (Romans 3:25).
“That he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).
“He entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12).
“Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins” (Hebrews 9:22).
doctrinalFocus:
The atonement is the work of Christ on the cross by which sinners are reconciled to God. The word itself means “at-one-ment,” the making of peace between two parties who were estranged. The Bible uses several pictures to describe what happened, and each adds something.

The first is sacrifice. In the Old Testament, an animal died in the place of the sinner, and its blood covered the guilt. Hebrews says that these sacrifices were a shadow. They could not take away sins, which is why they had to be repeated. Christ offered himself once for all, a perfect sacrifice. The second is substitution. Isaiah 53 says the Servant bore our iniquities and was pierced for our transgressions. He took our place. The penalty we deserved fell on him. This is sometimes called penal substitution: he bore the penalty in our place.

The third is propitiation. Romans 3:25 says God put forward Christ as a propitiation, a sacrifice that satisfies God’s righteous wrath against sin. This is not a picture of an angry God being calmed by a loving Son. It is God himself who puts forward the sacrifice, out of love. The Father, Son, and Spirit were united in this work. The fourth is redemption. A ransom price was paid to buy slaves out of bondage. Christ’s blood is the price (Mark 10:45; 1 Peter 1:18-19). The fifth is victory. Colossians 2:15 says that on the cross Christ triumphed over the rulers and authorities.

Romans 3:26 states the great puzzle that the cross solves: how can God be both just and the justifier of the ungodly? He cannot simply ignore sin, for he is righteous. The cross shows that he does not ignore it. The penalty is paid. And so God can freely forgive those who trust in Christ.

For believers, the atonement is the ground of our assurance. Our standing before God does not depend on our performance. It depends on what Christ has finished.
interpretation:
The three passages work like three voices in harmony. Isaiah gives the story in prophetic language. A righteous Servant suffers for others, though he did nothing wrong. The language is of sin-bearing and healing. “The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.” Notice that the Father is the one who lays it on him. This was not an accident or a tragedy. “It was the will of the LORD to crush him.” It was God’s plan, carried out in love.

Paul explains why this had to happen. All have sinned, and there is no distinction. No one can earn a place before God. But God offers justification as a gift. To justify means to declare righteous, a legal term. We are not made righteous by our deeds. God declares us righteous because of what Christ has done. This is received by faith, not earned. Paul also says that God “passed over former sins” in his forbearance, meaning that before the cross he had been patient with sin. The cross shows that this patience was not indifference. The debt was real, and it was finally paid.

Hebrews approaches it through the temple. The old high priest entered the Holy of Holies once a year with the blood of animals. Christ, by contrast, entered heaven itself with his own blood, once for all, “securing an eternal redemption.” The old covenant’s sacrifices only cleansed the flesh. Christ’s blood “purifies our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.” And he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance. Because he is both priest and sacrifice, nothing more needs to be offered.

Put together, these texts show that the cross was necessary, because sin is serious and God is just. It was sufficient, because Christ’s offering was perfect. And it was personal. The Servant bore “our” sins, and Christ gave himself “for me” (Galatians 2:20).
connection: Mark 10:45 says Christ came to give his life as a ransom for many. 2 Corinthians 5:21 says, “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.” Galatians 3:13 says Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. 1 John 2:2 and 4:10 speak of him as the propitiation for our sins. Ephesians 1:7 says that in him we have redemption through his blood. Hebrews 10:14 says that by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.
application:
Write down, in your own words, what Christ did on the cross for you. Use at least two of the pictures: sacrifice, substitution, ransom, victory.

Rest in the finished work. Ask where you are still trying to earn what has been given.

Share one of these truths with someone who is weighed down by guilt.
prayerPrompts: Thank the Father for laying on his Son the iniquity of all.
Thank Jesus for bearing your sins.
Tell God how you want to live in light of the cross.
